procedural_history.originating_court: The case originated as Writ Petitions (Nos. 289 to 295 of 1971) directly in the Supreme Court of India under Article 32 of the Constitution of India.
procedural_history.impugned_order: The petitioners challenged the validity of detention orders.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: There were no High Court proceedings mentioned in the text.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court held that the detention of the petitioners was illegal, made the rule issued in all the writ petitions absolute, and directed the release of the petitioners.

directions: The detention of the petitioners is illegal.
The petitioners are to be released forthwith unless they are required in connection with any other case.

issue.issue_text: Whether the unexplained delay by the State in considering and passing orders on the representation made by the petitioners violates their constitutional right under Article 22(5).

facts: The petitioners, who were detained, made a representation to the State Government on March 1, 1971.
The State Government received the representation on March 3, 1971, and rejected it on March 20, 1971.
This resulted in a delay of 17 days between the receipt and the disposal of the representation.
The petitioners specifically argued that this 17-day delay violated their constitutional right under Article 22(5).

The State contended that there was no delay, as it needed time to collect information to properly dispose of the representation, but it did not provide a satisfactory explanation for the 17-day period.
law: Article 22(5) of the Constitution guarantees a detenu the right to be afforded the "earliest opportunity" of making a representation against their detention order.

The Supreme Court, referencing its prior decisions (including *Durga Show v. The State of West Bengal* and *Jayanarayan Sukul v. State of West Bengal*), has established that this right implicitly requires the government to consider and dispose of such representations as expeditiously as possible.
An unexplained or unaccounted-for delay by the government in considering the representation is a violation of the constitutional right guaranteed under Article 22(5).
Such a violation is, by itself, a sufficient ground to declare the detention illegal and release the detenu.
application: The Court first established the fact of a 17-day delay, accepting the dates provided by the State.
It then noted that the State had a duty to explain this delay satisfactorily, especially since it was aware of the legal precedents holding that unexplained delays are unconstitutional.
The Court found that the State failed to provide a proper or satisfactory explanation for why it took 17 days to decide on the representation.

Applying the established legal principle, the Court held that this unexplained delay of 17 days directly violated the petitioners' constitutional right under Article 22(5), which requires expeditious consideration of their representation.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the unexplained 17-day delay by the State in disposing of the petitioners' representation constituted a violation of their constitutional right under Article 22(5). This violation alone was a sufficient reason to strike down the detention orders as illegal, and the Court ordered the petitioners to be released on this "short ground" without needing to examine the other merits of the case.

issue.issue_text: Whether the grounds of detention were vague or devoid of particulars.

facts: The petitioners argued that the grounds for their detention were vague, which made it impossible for them to make an effective representation against the detention order.
application: The Court decided to strike down the detention orders on a different, "short ground": an inordinate and unexplained delay by the government in considering the petitioners' representation.

Because the detention was already found to be illegal on the grounds of delay, the Court stated it was "unnecessary to pursue this aspect further" and did not need to refer to the grounds of detention in detail.
reasoning.conclusion: Despite not needing to rule definitively on the issue, the Court stated that "prima facie we are satisfied that the grounds are neither vague nor devoid of particulars." Therefore, the Court rejected the petitioners' argument on this specific point.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the unexplained delay by the State in considering and passing orders on the representation made by the petitioners violates their constitutional right under Article 22(5).
appellant_arguments: There was a delay by the State in passing orders on the representation made by the petitioners.
The delay has not been properly explained by the State.
The appropriate authority is constitutionally bound to consider a detenu's representation as early as possible, and any delay is an irresponsible and unconstitutional act.
respondent_arguments: There has been no delay on the part of the Government in considering the representation.
To properly dispose of the representation, certain information had to be collected from other officials, which took time.
Even if there was a delay, it has been properly explained in the counter-affidavit.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the grounds of detention were vague or devoid of particulars.
appellant_arguments: The matters mentioned in the grounds of detention are absolutely false.
The grounds of detention were vague and devoid of particulars.
respondent_arguments: The claim that the grounds were vague is absolutely unjustified.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An unexplained delay by the appropriate authority in considering a detenu's representation constitutes a violation of the constitutional right guaranteed under Article 22(5), and this circumstance by itself is a sufficient ground for holding the order of detention illegal.
obiter: The grounds of detention were prima facie neither vague nor devoid of particulars, and there were materials on which the detaining authority could have passed the detention orders.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: We have already held that there is an unexplained delay of 17 days between the date when the representation was received by the Administrator, namely, March 3, 1971 and when the latter c011sidered the representation and passed the order rejecting the same on March 20, 1971. If that is so, without anything more, that circumstance by itself is a sufficient ground for holding that the orders of detention of the petitioners are illegal and they are entitled to be released.
legal_tests_applied: The appropriate authority is bound to consider the representation of the detenu as early as possible.

The consideration of the representation of the detenu by the appropriate authority is entirely independent of any action by the Advisory Board including the consideration of the representation of the detenu by the Advisory Board.

There should not be any delay in the matter of consideration. It is true that no hard and fast rule can be laid down as to the measure of time taken by the appropriate authority for consideration but it has to be remembered that the Government has to be vigilant in the governance of the citizens.
The appropriate Government is to exercise its opinion and judgment on the representation before sending the case along with the detenu's representation to the Advisory Board.
why_appellant_lost: prima facie we are satisfied that the grounds are neither vague nor devoid of particulars, nor can it be said that in this case there were no materials on the basis of which the detaining authority could not have passed the orders of detention.
if there was any vagueness in all or any of the grounds, it was open to the petitioners to have asked for further particulars, which they did not do.
why_respondent_won: prima facie we are satisfied that the grounds are neither vague nor devoid of particulars, nor can it be said that in this case there were no materials on the basis of which the detaining authority could not have passed the orders of detention.
if there was any vagueness in all or any of the grounds, it was open to the petitioners to have asked for further particulars, which they did not do.
policy_considerations: The personal liberty of a person is at stake. Any delay would not only be an irresponsible act on the part of the appropriate authority but also unconstitutional because the Constitution enshrines the fundamental right of a detenu to have his representation considered and it is imperative that when the liberty of a person is in peril immediate action should be taken by the relevant authorities.
A citizen's right raises a correlative duty of the State.
